questions.stem:
A naive Bayes classifier has three classes with priors $P(C_1) = 0.5$, $P(C_2) = 0.3$, $P(C_3) = 0.2$. For a test point $x$ the class-conditional likelihoods are $P(x \mid C_1) = 0.2$, $P(x \mid C_2) = 0.5$, $P(x \mid C_3) = 0.6$.

The posterior $P(C_3 \mid x)$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Dropped the priors: $0.6/(0.2 + 0.5 + 0.6)$. $C_3$ is the least likely class a priori, so its posterior must be pulled down.
Stopped at the unnormalised score $0.2 \times 0.6$; divide by the sum of all three scores.
Returned the prior $P(C_3)$; the likelihood of $x$ was not used.

questions.solution:
1. Scores $P(c)P(x \mid c)$: $C_1$: $0.5 \times 0.2 = 0.10$; $C_2$: $0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$; $C_3$: $0.2 \times 0.6 = 0.12$.
2. Sum $= 0.37$.
3. $P(C_3 \mid x) = 0.12/0.37 \approx 0.32$. (The prediction is $C_2$, even though $C_3$ has the largest likelihood.)

questions.stem: A two-class Bayes classifier has priors $P(A) = 0.2$ and $P(B) = 0.8$. For an observed feature vector $x$, $P(x \mid A) = 0.6$ and $P(x \mid B) = 0.2$. Which class does it predict, and why?

options.text: $A$, because $P(x \mid A) > P(x \mid B)$
options.why: Compared likelihoods only and dropped the priors; class $B$ is four times as likely before seeing $x$.

options.text: $B$, because $0.8 \times 0.2 > 0.2 \times 0.6$
options.why: Scores prior × likelihood are $0.16$ for $B$ and $0.12$ for $A$; the larger score wins.

options.text: It cannot be decided without the evidence $P(x)$
options.why: $P(x)$ is the same denominator for both classes, so it cancels when comparing them.

options.text: $B$, because a class with prior above $0.5$ is always predicted
options.why: The prior alone does not decide; a strong enough likelihood ratio can overturn it. Here it simply does not.

questions.solution:
1. Score$(A) = 0.2 \times 0.6 = 0.12$; Score$(B) = 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.16$.
2. $0.16 > 0.12$, so predict $B$ ($P(B \mid x) = 0.16/0.28 \approx 0.57$).
3. $P(x)$ is common to both and is not needed for the decision.

questions.stem:
A Bernoulli naive Bayes classifier with two binary features is trained on 10 messages: 4 of class Pos and 6 of class Neg.

- $F_1$ is present in 3 of the 4 Pos messages and in 0 of the 6 Neg messages.
- $F_2$ is present in 1 of the 4 Pos messages and in 3 of the 6 Neg messages.

Priors are the class frequencies. Each feature likelihood uses Laplace smoothing (add 1 to the count of each of the two outcomes, present/absent). For a new message with $F_1 = 1$ and $F_2 = 0$, the posterior $P(\text{Neg} \mid x)$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: No smoothing: $P(F_1{=}1 \mid \text{Neg}) = 0/6$ zeroes the whole Neg score. Smoothing gives it $1/8$.
Added 1 to the denominator instead of 2 (the number of outcomes): $(n + 1)/(N_c + 1)$.
Dropped the priors $0.4$ and $0.6$ and normalised the likelihood products only.
Reported $P(\text{Pos} \mid x)$; the question asks for Neg.

questions.solution:
1. Smoothed likelihoods ($+1$ on top, $+2$ below): Pos: $P(F_1{=}1) = 4/6$, $P(F_2{=}0) = 4/6$. Neg: $P(F_1{=}1) = 1/8$, $P(F_2{=}0) = 4/8$.
2. Pos score $= 0.4 \times \frac46 \times \frac46 \approx 0.1778$; Neg score $= 0.6 \times \frac18 \times \frac48 = 0.0375$.
3. $P(\text{Neg} \mid x) = 0.0375/(0.1778 + 0.0375) \approx 0.17$.

questions.stem:
A multinomial naive Bayes text classifier has equal priors and uses Laplace (add-one) smoothing over a vocabulary of $V = 4$ words. Word counts in the training data:

| word | spam | ham |
|---|---|---|
| cheap | 4 | 1 |
| meeting | 0 | 3 |
| offer | 3 | 0 |
| report | 1 | 4 |
| **total** | 8 | 8 |

The new document is "cheap cheap meeting". Which statement is correct?

options.text: Ham, with probability 1, because *meeting* never occurs in spam
options.why: That is the unsmoothed estimate $0/8$. With add-one smoothing $P(\textit{meeting} \mid \text{spam}) = 1/12$, not 0.

options.text: Ham, with $P(\text{ham} \mid d) = 8/13$
options.why: Counted *cheap* only once. In the multinomial model each occurrence contributes its own factor.

options.text: Spam, with $P(\text{spam} \mid d) = 25/29$
options.why: Dropped the token *meeting*; its factor $1/12$ vs $4/12$ strongly favours ham.

options.text: Spam, with $P(\text{spam} \mid d) = 25/41$

questions.solution:
1. Smoothed: $P(w \mid c) = (\text{count} + 1)/(8 + 4)$. Spam: cheap $5/12$, meeting $1/12$. Ham: cheap $2/12$, meeting $4/12$.
2. Spam score $\propto (5/12)^2 \cdot (1/12) = 25/1728$; ham $\propto (2/12)^2 \cdot (4/12) = 16/1728$ (equal priors cancel).
3. $P(\text{spam} \mid d) = 25/41 \approx 0.61$: predict spam.

questions.stem: Which statements about the naive Bayes classifier are true?

options.text: Naive Bayes is a discriminative model that learns $P(y \mid x)$ directly
options.why: Swapped: NB is generative; it learns $P(y)$ and $P(x \mid y)$ and gets the posterior through Bayes' rule.

options.text: If $P(x_j = v \mid c)$ is the same for every class $c$, observing $x_j = v$ does not change the posterior
options.why: The same factor multiplies every class score, so it cancels on normalising.

options.text: Naive Bayes can only be applied when the features really are conditionally independent given the class
options.why: The assumption simplifies the model; NB is often used (and often classifies well) when it is violated.

options.text: To find the predicted class, the evidence $P(x)$ need not be computed
options.why: $P(x)$ is a common denominator; comparing the numerators $P(c)\prod_j P(x_j \mid c)$ is enough.

questions.solution:
1. A factor equal across classes cancels in the normalisation, so it carries no evidence.
2. The argmax only needs $P(c)\prod_j P(x_j \mid c)$; $P(x)$ is the same for all classes.
3. NB is generative, not discriminative.
4. Conditional independence is a modelling assumption, not a requirement for using NB.

questions.stem: A naive Bayes classifier has 2 classes and 10 binary features. Counting the class prior and all class-conditional feature probabilities, the number of **independent** parameters it must estimate is ______.

traps.why: Counted the feature probabilities but forgot the one free prior parameter $P(C_1)$.
Counted $P(x_j{=}0 \mid c)$ and $P(x_j{=}1 \mid c)$ separately; they sum to 1, so only one is free.
Counted both priors; $P(C_2) = 1 - P(C_1)$ is not free.
Counted the full joint table $2(2^{10} - 1) + 1$; avoiding that is exactly what the naive assumption buys.

questions.solution:
1. Prior: one free number $P(C_1)$.
2. For each class and each binary feature, one number $P(x_j{=}1 \mid c)$: $2 \times 10 = 20$.
3. Total $= 20 + 1 = 21$ (versus $2(2^{10} - 1) + 1 = 2047$ for the full joint model).

questions.stem: A Gaussian naive Bayes classifier with one feature has equal priors and class-conditional densities $X \mid A \sim N(2, 1)$ and $X \mid B \sim N(5, 4)$ (the second parameter is the variance). For $x = 3$, the posterior $P(A \mid x)$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Dropped the factor $1/\sigma$ in the Gaussian density. The exponents are equal here, so only the $1/\sigma$ factors ($1$ vs $1/2$) separate the classes.
Used $\sigma = 2$ instead of $\sigma^2 = 4$ in the exponent: $e^{-(3-5)^2/(2 \cdot 2)}$.
Read 4 as the standard deviation, so used variance 16 for class $B$.

questions.stem: A Bernoulli naive Bayes classifier (each word is a binary present/absent feature, vocabulary of 50 words) is trained with Laplace smoothing. Class $c$ has 8 training documents, and the word *refund* appears in none of them. The estimate of $P(\textit{refund} \text{ present} \mid c)$ is

options.why: The unsmoothed estimate $0/8$; smoothing exists to avoid this zero.
Added 1 to the denominator; a binary feature has 2 outcomes, so add 2.
$(0 + 1)/(8 + 2)$: one pseudo-count for each of the two outcomes, present and absent.
Used the vocabulary size $V = 50$, which is the multinomial rule. Here each word is its own two-valued feature.

questions.solution:
1. Each word is a binary feature with 2 values, so Laplace smoothing adds 1 to each value's count and 2 to the denominator.
2. $P = (0 + 1)/(8 + 2) = 1/10$.

questions.stem: A classifier has three classes with priors $0.2, 0.3, 0.5$ for $C_1, C_2, C_3$. For a test point $x$, $P(x \mid C_1) = 0.5$, $P(x \mid C_2) = 0.4$, $P(x \mid C_3) = 0.1$. The classifier predicts the class with the largest posterior. According to the model, the probability that this prediction is wrong is

options.why: That is the maximum posterior itself; the error is $1 - \max$.
Ignored the priors: likelihoods $0.5, 0.4, 0.1$ give max posterior $0.5$ for $C_1$.
Subtracted the unnormalised score $0.12$ from 1; normalise by $0.27$ first.

questions.stem: Which statements about computing and smoothing naive Bayes scores are true?

options.text: Choosing the class with the largest $\log P(c) + \sum_j \log P(x_j \mid c)$ gives the same prediction as comparing the products
options.why: $\log$ is strictly increasing, so the argmax is unchanged; logs also avoid numerical underflow.

options.text: Smoothing can change the predicted class only when some count is zero
options.why: Smoothing changes every ratio. Counts $1/1$ vs $5/10$ favour the first class, but with $V = 10$ they become $2/11$ vs $6/20$ and favour the second.

options.text: Naive Bayes needs the full table $P(x_1, \dots, x_d \mid c)$, so its parameter count grows exponentially in $d$
options.why: Swapped with the full Bayes model; NB stores one distribution per feature, so it grows linearly in $d$.

options.text: With add-$\alpha$ smoothing over a vocabulary of size $V$, every $P(w \mid c) \to 1/V$ as $\alpha \to \infty$
options.why: $(n_w + \alpha)/(N_c + \alpha V) \to \alpha/(\alpha V) = 1/V$: the data are swamped by the pseudo-counts.

questions.solution:
1. Logs preserve order, so log-scores give the same argmax and avoid underflow.
2. $(n_w + \alpha)/(N_c + \alpha V) \to 1/V$ as $\alpha$ grows.
3. Smoothing alters all estimates; it can flip a decision even when no count is zero.
4. NB's factorisation makes the parameter count linear in $d$.

questions.stem:
Two classes have mean difference $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = (4, -2)$ and pooled within-class scatter matrix
$$S_W = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.$$
The Fisher LDA direction, rescaled to the form $w = (1, a)$, has $a =$ ______.

traps.why: Used $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = (4, -2)$ directly, without $S_W^{-1}$.
Multiplied by $S_W$ instead of $S_W^{-1}$: $(8, -2)$.
Gave $(1, 1)$, which is perpendicular to $w$: a direction along the boundary, not the projection direction.

questions.stem: Two classes in $\mathbb{R}^2$ are Gaussian with different means, class 1 with covariance $I$ and class 2 with covariance $4I$. Priors are equal. The Bayes-optimal decision boundary between them is

options.text: a straight line, as in LDA
options.why: LDA's line needs one shared covariance. Here the $\lVert x\rVert^2$ terms have coefficients $-\frac12$ and $-\frac18$, so they do not cancel.

options.text: a circle
options.why: The log-ratio keeps $-\frac38\lVert x\rVert^2$ plus linear terms; an isotropic quadratic set to a constant is a circle (QDA case).

options.text: the perpendicular bisector of the two means
options.why: That is the boundary only for equal priors and a shared spherical covariance.

options.text: nonexistent, since class 2 has the larger covariance and wins everywhere
options.why: Near $\mu_1$ the tighter class 1 density is much larger, so class 1 wins there; a boundary must exist.

questions.solution:
1. $\ln p_1(x) - \ln p_2(x) = -\frac12\lVert x - \mu_1\rVert^2 + \frac18\lVert x - \mu_2\rVert^2 + \text{const}$.
2. The $\lVert x\rVert^2$ coefficient is $-\frac12 + \frac18 = -\frac38 \ne 0$, so the boundary is quadratic.
3. Both covariances are multiples of $I$, so the quadratic part is $\lVert x\rVert^2$ and the boundary is a circle.

questions.stem: One-feature LDA: class 1 has $X \sim N(10, 9)$ and class 2 has $X \sim N(4, 9)$ (variance 9 in both). Priors are $P(1) = 0.2$ and $P(2) = 0.8$. The classifier predicts class 1 for $x$ above a threshold $t$ and class 2 below it. The value of $t$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Midpoint of the means; correct only for equal priors.
Shifted the wrong way. Class 2 is more likely, so its region grows and the threshold moves toward class 1's mean 10.
Used $\sigma = 3$ instead of $\sigma^2 = 9$ in the shift term.

questions.stem:
Two classes have means $\mu_1 = (2, 3)$ and $\mu_2 = (0, 1)$ and pooled within-class scatter
$$S_W = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Up to a non-zero scale factor, the Fisher LDA projection direction is

options.why: Used $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = (2, 2)$ alone, which is optimal only when $S_W$ is a multiple of $I$.
Multiplied by $S_W$: $S_W(2, 2) = (12, 8)$. Fisher uses $S_W^{-1}$.
Perpendicular to the mean difference: a boundary direction, not a projection direction.
$S_W^{-1} = \frac14\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ maps $(2, 2)$ to $(0, 1)$: the spread along $x_1$ is so large that only $x_2$ is used.

questions.stem:
Two classes have mean difference $d = \mu_1 - \mu_2 = (3, 1)$ and within-class scatter $S_W = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The Fisher criterion is
$$J(w) = \frac{(w^\top d)^2}{w^\top S_W w}.$$
The maximum value of $J(w)$ over all non-zero $w$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Evaluated $J$ at $w = d$ instead of the optimal $w = S_W^{-1}d$: $100/19$.
Computed $d^\top S_W d$; the maximum is $d^\top S_W^{-1} d$.
Forgot to square $w^\top d$ in the numerator: $5.5/5.5$.

questions.stem: Fisher LDA is applied to a labelled data set with 4 classes and 10 features (and many more points than features). The largest number of useful discriminant directions it can produce is

options.why: Counted one direction per class; the 4 deviations from the overall mean sum to zero, so only 3 are independent.
Applied "minus one" to the number of features instead of the number of classes.
The between-class scatter is built from 4 means around their overall mean, so its rank is at most $4 - 1$.
That is the PCA limit (number of features); LDA is limited by the classes.

questions.solution:
1. $S_B = \sum_k n_k(\mu_k - \mu)(\mu_k - \mu)^\top$ with $\sum_k n_k(\mu_k - \mu) = 0$.
2. So $\operatorname{rank} S_B \le K - 1 = 3$, and at most $\min(K - 1, d) = 3$ directions exist.

questions.stem: Which statements comparing LDA, QDA and Gaussian naive Bayes are true?

options.text: LDA's boundary is linear only when the class priors are equal
options.why: Priors only add the constant $\ln(\pi_1/\pi_2)$; the boundary stays a hyperplane.

options.text: QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix for each class, so with few points per class it tends to have higher variance than LDA
options.why: More parameters ($K$ full covariances instead of one) are estimated from the same data.

options.text: Gaussian naive Bayes whose per-feature variances are shared by all classes is a special case of LDA with a diagonal covariance
options.why: Shared $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2, \dots, \sigma_d^2)$ for every class is exactly LDA with a diagonal $\Sigma$, so the boundary is linear.

options.text: Converting one feature from metres to centimetres changes LDA's predicted labels
options.why: LDA is unchanged by an invertible linear rescaling: the means and $\Sigma$ rescale together and the discriminant is the same.

questions.solution:
1. QDA has $K$ covariance matrices to estimate, so it overfits more easily with little data.
2. A shared diagonal covariance is a special case of LDA's shared $\Sigma$.
3. Unequal priors shift the LDA hyperplane but do not bend it.
4. Rescaling $x' = Ax$ gives $\mu' = A\mu$, $\Sigma' = A\Sigma A^\top$, and $(x' - \mu')^\top\Sigma'^{-1}(x' - \mu') = (x - \mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu)$: same predictions.

questions.stem: Class $A$ has points $(1, 2)$, $(3, 4)$ and class $B$ has points $(5, 1)$, $(7, 1)$, $(6, 4)$. The within-class scatter matrix is $S_W = S_A + S_B$, where $S_k = \sum_{x \in k}(x - \mu_k)(x - \mu_k)^\top$. The $(2, 2)$ entry of $S_W$ (the second-feature diagonal entry) is ______.

traps.why: Used only class $B$'s scatter; $S_W$ adds both classes.
Computed the total scatter around the overall mean $2.4$; within-class scatter uses each class's own mean.
Divided by the number of points; the scatter defined here is a sum, not an average.

questions.solution:
1. Class $A$: second-feature mean $3$; deviations $-1, 1$; sum of squares $2$.
2. Class $B$: second-feature mean $2$; deviations $-1, -1, 2$; sum of squares $6$.
3. $(S_W)_{22} = 2 + 6 = 8$.

questions.stem: One-feature LDA: two Gaussian classes share a variance, with means $\mu_1 < \mu_2$. The prior of class 1 is raised from $0.5$ to $0.7$. Which statements are true?

options.text: The threshold moves toward $\mu_2$
options.why: Class 1 becomes more likely, so it claims more of the line; its region extends toward class 2.

options.text: The threshold moves toward $\mu_1$
options.why: Direction reversed: that would shrink the region of the class that just became more likely.

options.text: The boundary is still a single threshold (a linear boundary)
options.why: The prior adds only a constant to the log-ratio; the $x^2$ terms still cancel.

options.text: In the $d$-dimensional version of this model, the boundary's normal vector $\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1 - \mu_2)$ changes with the priors
options.why: The priors only change the offset $b$; the normal vector depends on the means and $\Sigma$ alone.

questions.solution:
1. Threshold $t = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2\ln(\pi_1/\pi_2)}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}$; with $\pi_1 > \pi_2$ and $\mu_2 > \mu_1$ the shift is positive, toward $\mu_2$.
2. The boundary stays linear; in $d$ dimensions only the offset changes.

questions.stem: Two Gaussian classes in $\mathbb{R}^2$ share the covariance $\Sigma = I$. Class 1 has mean $(0, 0)$ and prior $0.75$; class 2 has mean $(2, 2)$ and prior $0.25$. The LDA boundary is a line $x_1 + x_2 = c$. It crosses the $x_1$-axis at $x_1 =$ ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Used the perpendicular bisector of the means, which ignores the unequal priors.
Shifted toward class 1; the more likely class 1 should gain territory, pushing the line toward $(2, 2)$.
Forgot to divide $\ln 3$ by 2 when going from $2x_1 + 2x_2 = 4 + \ln 3$ to $x_1 + x_2 = c$.

questions.solution:
1. Equal scores: $-\frac12\lVert x\rVert^2 + \ln 0.75 = -\frac12\lVert x - \mu_2\rVert^2 + \ln 0.25$.
2. The $\lVert x\rVert^2$ terms cancel: $\mu_2^\top x = \frac12\lVert\mu_2\rVert^2 + \ln 3$, i.e. $2x_1 + 2x_2 = 4 + \ln 3$.
3. $x_1 + x_2 = 2 + \frac{\ln 3}{2} \approx 2.55$; at $x_2 = 0$, $x_1 \approx 2.55$.

questions.stem:
A labelled data set has 8 points:

| class | points |
|---|---|
| $A$ | $(-4, 0.5)$, $(-4, 1.5)$, $(4, 0.5)$, $(4, 1.5)$ |
| $B$ | $(-4, -0.5)$, $(-4, -1.5)$, $(4, -0.5)$, $(4, -1.5)$ |

PCA (on all 8 points, labels ignored) and Fisher LDA (using labels) each pick one direction. Which is correct?

options.text: Both pick the $x_2$-axis
options.why: PCA ignores labels; it follows the largest total spread, which is along $x_1$.

options.text: PCA picks the $x_1$-axis; LDA picks the $x_2$-axis
options.why: Total variance is largest along $x_1$ (scatter 128 vs 10), but the class means differ only along $x_2$, where within-class spread is small.

options.text: PCA picks the $x_2$-axis; LDA picks the $x_1$-axis
options.why: The two methods' goals are swapped.

options.text: Both pick the $x_1$-axis
options.why: Treated LDA as a variance maximiser like PCA; along $x_1$ the two classes overlap completely.

questions.solution:
1. Overall mean is $(0, 0)$. Total scatter: $x_1$: $8 \times 16 = 128$; $x_2$: $4(0.25 + 2.25) = 10$; no cross term. PCA's first direction is $x_1$.
2. Class means $(0, 1)$ and $(0, -1)$; $S_W = \operatorname{diag}(128, 2)$.
3. $w \propto S_W^{-1}(0, 2) = (0, 1)$: LDA picks $x_2$.

questions.stem: A hard-margin linear SVM in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has $w = (1, 2, 2)$ and $b = 5$, with margin hyperplanes $w^\top x + b = \pm 1$. The distance between the two margin hyperplanes is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Computed $1/\lVert w\rVert$, the half-width from the boundary to one margin hyperplane.
Used $2/\lVert w\rVert^2 = 2/9$; the width uses the norm, not its square.
Used the $\ell_1$ norm $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ instead of the Euclidean norm.

questions.solution:
1. $\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$ (the bias $b$ does not affect the width).
2. Width $= 2/\lVert w\rVert = 2/3 \approx 0.67$.

questions.stem: A linear classifier has decision function $f(x) = x_1 - 2x_2 + 3$. For the point $(1, 4)$, which statement is correct?

options.text: Its distance from the boundary is $4/5$
options.why: Divided by $\lVert w\rVert^2 = 5$ instead of $\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt 5$.

options.text: Its distance from the boundary is $4/\sqrt 5$, on the side where $f(x) > 0$
options.why: Took the absolute value before reading the side; $f = -4$ is negative.

options.text: Its distance from the boundary is $4/\sqrt 5 \approx 1.79$, on the side where $f(x) < 0$
options.why: $f(1, 4) = 1 - 8 + 3 = -4$ and $\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt 5$; the negative sign gives the side.

options.text: Its distance from the boundary is $4/3$
options.why: Divided by the $\ell_1$ norm $|1| + |-2| = 3$ instead of the Euclidean norm.

questions.solution:
1. $f(1, 4) = 1 - 8 + 3 = -4$, so the point is on the negative side.
2. $\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt 5$.
3. Distance $= |{-4}|/\sqrt 5 \approx 1.79$.

questions.stem: A hard-margin linear SVM is trained on only two points: $x_+ = (3, 1)$ with label $+1$ and $x_- = (1, -1)$ with label $-1$. Its decision function is scaled so that $f(x_+) = 1$ and $f(x_-) = -1$. For the new point $P = (5, 2)$, the value $f(P) = w^\top P + b$ is ______ (round to one decimal).

traps.why: Took $w = x_+ - x_- = (2, 2)$ without rescaling (with $b = -4$ from the midpoint); then $f(x_+) = 4$, not 1.
Gave the geometric distance $f(P)/\lVert w\rVert$ of $P$ from the boundary, not the value of $f$.
Used $w = (1, 1)$, $b = -2$: the right boundary, but then $f(x_+) = 2$. The condition $f(x_\pm) = \pm 1$ forces a factor $\frac12$.

questions.stem:
A hard-margin linear SVM is trained on

| class | points |
|---|---|
| $+1$ | $(3, 0)$, $(3, 2)$, $(5, 1)$ |
| $-1$ | $(1, 1)$, $(0, 3)$, $(-1, 0)$ |

and learns $f(x) = x_1 - 2$. Deleting which **one** of the following points from the training set leaves $w$ and $b$ unchanged?

options.why: It is the only negative point on $f = -1$; without it the nearest negative point is farther away and the margin grows.
It is a support vector ($f = 1$). Without it the line can tilt and the margin widens from 2 to $\sqrt 5$.
Also a support vector; by symmetry, removing it lets the line tilt the other way to margin $\sqrt 5$.
$y f = -(0 - 2) = 2 > 1$: it lies outside the margin, its constraint is inactive and $\alpha = 0$.

questions.solution:
1. $y f(x)$: $(3,0)$: 1; $(3,2)$: 1; $(5,1)$: 3; $(1,1)$: 1; $(0,3)$: 2; $(-1,0)$: 3.
2. Support vectors (those with $y f = 1$): $(3,0)$, $(3,2)$, $(1,1)$.
3. Removing a non-support vector such as $(0, 3)$ leaves the solution unchanged. Removing any of the three support vectors lets the margin grow (to $\sqrt 5$ or $\sqrt{10}$).

questions.stem: A hard-margin linear SVM has been trained on a linearly separable data set. Which statements are true?

options.text: The margin width depends on how many support vectors there are
options.why: The width is $2/\lVert w\rVert$; it depends on where the closest points are, not how many lie on the margin.

options.text: The boundary lies closer to the class that has more training points
options.why: The SVM boundary sits halfway between the margin hyperplanes; class sizes do not enter.

options.text: Adding a new point that is correctly classified and lies outside the margin leaves the solution unchanged
options.why: Its constraint $y f \ge 1$ already holds strictly, so the old optimum is still feasible and optimal.

options.text: Adding a new point of the correct class that lies strictly inside the margin forces the solution to change
options.why: It has $y f < 1$, so the old $(w, b)$ violates its constraint and is no longer feasible.

questions.solution:
1. A point outside the margin adds an inactive constraint: nothing changes.
2. A point inside the margin violates the current constraints, so the optimum must move.
3. Width $2/\lVert w\rVert$ is set by the geometry of the closest points.
4. The boundary is equidistant from both margin hyperplanes, regardless of class counts.

questions.stem:
A linear classifier $f(x) = 2x_1 + x_2 - 4$ (not necessarily an SVM) is applied to

| point | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | label |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 3 | 2 | +1 |
| B | 2 | 1 | +1 |
| C | 1 | 0 | −1 |
| D | 0 | 1 | −1 |

Its geometric margin on this data, $\min_i y_i f(x_i)/\lVert w\rVert$, is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Reported the functional margin $\min y_i f(x_i)$ without dividing by $\lVert w\rVert$.
Used the SVM width formula $2/\lVert w\rVert$; the geometric margin is the smallest point distance, $1/\sqrt 5$ here.
Divided by $\lVert w\rVert^2 = 5$ instead of $\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt 5$.

questions.solution:
1. $y f$: A $= 4$, B $= 1$, C $= -(2 - 4) = 2$, D $= -(1 - 4) = 3$. All positive, so all are correct.
2. Minimum $= 1$ (point B); $\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt 5$.
3. Geometric margin $= 1/\sqrt 5 \approx 0.45$.

questions.stem: Training points $(x_i, y_i)$ with $y_i \in \{-1, +1\}$ are linearly separable. Which optimisation problem gives the hard-margin (maximum-margin) linear SVM?

options.text: $\max_{w,b} \lVert w\rVert^2$ subject to $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1$ for all $i$
options.why: Direction reversed: a larger $\lVert w\rVert$ means a narrower margin (and the problem is unbounded).

options.text: $\min_{w,b} \frac12\lVert w\rVert^2$ subject to $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 0$ for all $i$
options.why: With right-hand side 0, $w = 0$, $b = 0$ is feasible and optimal; the margin scale is lost.

options.text: $\min_{w,b} \frac12\lVert w\rVert^2$ subject to $w^\top x_i + b \ge 1$ for all $i$
options.why: Dropped the label $y_i$: this forces every point onto the positive side.

options.text: $\min_{w,b} \frac12\lVert w\rVert^2$ subject to $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1$ for all $i$
options.why: Fixing the functional margin at 1 makes the geometric margin $2/\lVert w\rVert$; minimising $\lVert w\rVert$ maximises it.

questions.solution:
1. The constraint $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1$ puts every point on its correct side, at least on its margin hyperplane.
2. The margin width is $2/\lVert w\rVert$, so maximising it is minimising $\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2$.

questions.stem: A hard-margin linear SVM is trained on only two points: $(4, 5)$ with label $+1$ and $(1, 1)$ with label $-1$. The norm $\lVert w\rVert$ of the learned weight vector is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Gave the margin width (the distance between the two points) instead of $\lVert w\rVert$.
Gave the half-width $1/\lVert w\rVert$, the distance from the boundary to each point.
Set $1/\lVert w\rVert$ equal to the full width 5; it is the half-width.

questions.solution:
1. With two points, both are support vectors and the margin width equals their distance: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$.
2. Width $= 2/\lVert w\rVert = 5$, so $\lVert w\rVert = 2/5 = 0.4$.

questions.stem: A linear classifier has $f(x) = x_1 + x_2 - 3$, with margin hyperplanes $f(x) = \pm 1$. Which statements are true?

options.text: The point $(1, 1)$ with label $-1$ lies strictly inside the margin
options.why: $f(1, 1) = -1$, so $y f = 1$: it is exactly on the margin hyperplane, not inside.

options.text: The point $(2, 2)$ with label $+1$ lies on the margin hyperplane $f = +1$
options.why: $f(2, 2) = 1$ exactly, so $y f = 1$.

options.text: The point $(3, 3)$ with label $-1$ is correctly classified because $|f| = 3 > 1$
options.why: The side is decided by the sign of $y f = -3 < 0$: misclassified, and far on the wrong side.

options.text: The point $(2, 1.5)$ with label $+1$ is correctly classified but lies inside the margin
options.why: $f = 0.5$: positive (correct side) but $y f = 0.5 < 1$.

questions.solution:
1. Compute $y f$: $(2,2)$, $+1$: $1$ (on margin). $(1,1)$, $-1$: $1$ (on margin).
2. $(2, 1.5)$, $+1$: $0.5$, so $0 < y f < 1$: correct side, inside the margin.
3. $(3,3)$, $-1$: $-3 < 0$: misclassified.

questions.stem: A hard-margin linear SVM on one feature is trained on positive points $x = 4, 6$ and negative points $x = 0, 1$, with decision function $f(x) = wx + b$ scaled so that the support vectors satisfy $y f(x) = 1$. Then $(w, b)$ is

options.why: Right boundary ($2.5$), but set $1/w$ equal to the full gap 3; the gap is $2/w$.
Support vectors $1$ and $4$: $w + b = -1$ and $4w + b = 1$ give $w = 2/3$, $b = -5/3$; boundary at $2.5$.
Sign slip on $b$: this puts the boundary at $x = -2.5$, with every point on the positive side.
Right boundary, but scale not fixed: $f(4) = 1.5 \ne 1$, so the support vectors are not on $f = \pm 1$.

questions.solution:
1. The closest opposite pair is $1$ (negative) and $4$ (positive): these are the support vectors, and the boundary is at their midpoint $2.5$.
2. $4w + b = 1$ and $w + b = -1$: subtracting, $3w = 2$, so $w = 2/3$ and $b = -5/3$.
3. Check: width $2/w = 3 = 4 - 1$.

questions.stem: In a soft-margin linear SVM, a training point with label $y = -1$ gets the score $f(x) = w^\top x + b = 0.3$. Its hinge loss (the optimal slack $\xi$ for this point) is ______ (round to one decimal).

traps.why: Used the perceptron loss $\max(0, -yf)$; the hinge adds the margin: $\max(0, 1 - yf)$.
Dropped the label: computed $1 - f$ instead of $1 - yf = 1 + 0.3$.
Treated the point as fine because $|f| < 1$; with $y = -1$ and $f > 0$ it is on the wrong side.

questions.solution:
1. $y f(x) = (-1)(0.3) = -0.3$.
2. $\xi = \max(0, 1 - (-0.3)) = 1.3$. Since $\xi > 1$, the point is misclassified.

questions.stem: At the optimum of a soft-margin SVM, a training point has slack $\xi_i = 0.4$. This point is

options.text: misclassified
options.why: Misclassification needs $y f < 0$, i.e. $\xi > 1$. Here $y f = 0.6 > 0$.

options.text: correctly classified but inside the margin
options.why: $y f = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6$, which lies between 0 and 1.

options.text: outside the margin, so it is not a support vector
options.why: Outside the margin means $\xi = 0$. A point with $\xi > 0$ is a margin violator and is a support vector ($\alpha_i = C$).

options.text: exactly on the decision boundary $f = 0$
options.why: That needs $y f = 0$, i.e. $\xi = 1$.

questions.solution:
1. $\xi_i = \max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i)) = 0.4$ gives $y_i f(x_i) = 0.6$.
2. $0 < y f < 1$: correct side, inside the margin. (Ranges: $\xi = 0$ outside or on the margin; $0 < \xi \le 1$ inside, correct side or on the boundary; $\xi > 1$ misclassified.)

questions.stem:
One-feature data: negative points $x = 0, 1.5$ and positive points $x = 2, 4$. Two candidate classifiers $f(x) = wx + b$ are compared under the soft-margin objective $\frac12 w^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i$, with $\xi_i = \max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i))$:

- Candidate P: $w = 4$, $b = -7$.
- Candidate Q: $w = 1$, $b = -2$.

The value of $C$ at which P and Q have the same objective value is ______.

traps.why: Dropped the $\frac12$ in front of $w^2$: $(16 - 1)/1.5$.
Counted the 2 violating points instead of summing their slacks $0.5 + 1$.
Gave the point $x = 2$ (with $f = 0$, on Q's boundary) zero slack; its slack is $1 - 0 = 1$.

questions.solution:
1. P: $f = 4x - 7$ gives $y f = 7, 1, 1, 9$: all slacks 0. Objective $= \frac12(16) = 8$.
2. Q: $f = x - 2$ gives $y f = 2, 0.5, 0, 2$: slacks $0, 0.5, 1, 0$, sum $1.5$. Objective $= 0.5 + 1.5C$.
3. $0.5 + 1.5C = 8 \Rightarrow C = 5$. (For $C > 5$ the zero-slack P wins; for $C < 5$ the wider-margin Q wins.)

questions.stem:
A linear soft-margin SVM is trained with two values of $C$ on the same data:

| $C$ | training error | validation error |
|---|---|---|
| $0.01$ | 30% | 31% |
| $1000$ | 0% | 25% |

Which diagnosis is correct?

options.text: $C = 0.01$ underfits (wide margin, high bias); $C = 1000$ overfits (narrow margin, high variance)
options.why: Tiny $C$ makes slack cheap, so the fit is loose and both errors are high; huge $C$ fits the training set exactly but generalises worse than it trains.

options.text: $C = 0.01$ overfits and $C = 1000$ underfits
options.why: Direction of $C$ reversed: small $C$ tolerates violations (more regularisation), large $C$ does not.

options.text: Both models have the same margin, because $C$ affects only the slacks, not $w$
options.why: $C$ trades $\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2$ against the slacks, so it changes $w$ and hence the margin $2/\lVert w\rVert$.

options.text: To close the train–validation gap of the $C = 1000$ model, increase $C$ further
options.why: A larger $C$ penalises violations even more and fits the training data even more tightly; to reduce variance, decrease $C$.

questions.solution:
1. Small $C$: violations are cheap, so the margin is wide and the model is simple; high training and validation error mean high bias.
2. Large $C$: violations are expensive, so the margin is narrow; 0% training but 25% validation error is a variance gap.
3. A value of $C$ in between is likely best.

questions.stem: Which statements about the hinge loss $\ell(y, f) = \max(0, 1 - y f)$ are true?

options.text: It is zero whenever $y f \ge 1$
options.why: Then $1 - y f \le 0$, so the max is 0: points on or beyond their margin cost nothing.

options.text: It is convex in $(w, b)$ for a linear $f = w^\top x + b$
options.why: It is the maximum of two affine functions of $(w, b)$, which is convex.

options.text: It equals the 0–1 loss on every point
options.why: Hinge is a convex upper bound of the 0–1 loss; e.g. $y f = 0.5$ gives hinge $0.5$ but 0–1 loss $0$.

options.text: A correctly classified point always has zero hinge loss
options.why: A correct point with $0 < y f < 1$ is inside the margin and pays $1 - y f > 0$.

questions.solution:
1. $y f \ge 1 \Rightarrow$ loss 0.
2. $\max(0, 1 - y(w^\top x + b))$ is a max of affine functions: convex.
3. Hinge is a convex upper bound on the 0–1 loss, not equal to it: at $y f = 0.5$ hinge is $0.5$ while the 0–1 loss is 0.
4. So a correctly classified point inside the margin ($0 < y f < 1$) still pays a positive hinge loss.

questions.stem: For $x = (1, 2)$ and $z = (4, -1)$, the polynomial kernel $K(x, z) = (1 + x^\top z)^3$ equals ______.

traps.why: Dropped the constant 1: $(x^\top z)^3 = 2^3$.
Used power 2 instead of 3, or put the 1 outside the bracket: $1 + 2^3$.
Forgot to raise $1 + x^\top z$ to the power 3.

questions.stem: For inputs $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$, the kernel $K(x, z) = (1 + x^\top z)^2$ equals $\phi(x)^\top\phi(z)$ for a feature map $\phi$ with the smallest possible number of components. How many components does $\phi(x)$ have?

options.why: Counted only the degree-2 monomials; $(1 + x^\top z)^2$ also contains degree-0 and degree-1 terms.
Counted $x_ix_j$ and $x_jx_i$ as separate features; each cross pair appears once, with weight $\sqrt 2$.
Forgot the constant feature that comes from the 1 inside the bracket.
One constant, 3 linear terms $\sqrt2 x_i$, 3 squares $x_i^2$ and 3 cross terms $\sqrt2 x_ix_j$ ($i < j$): $\binom{3+2}{2} = 10$.

questions.solution:
1. $(1 + x^\top z)^2 = 1 + 2\sum_i x_iz_i + \sum_i x_i^2z_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_jz_iz_j$.
2. Matching features: $1$; $\sqrt2 x_i$ (3); $x_i^2$ (3); $\sqrt2 x_ix_j$ for $i < j$ (3).
3. Total $1 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 10$.

questions.stem: An SVM uses the RBF kernel $K(x, z) = \exp(-\gamma\lVert x - z\rVert^2)$. What happens as $\gamma$ is made very large?

options.text: The boundary becomes smoother and close to linear
options.why: Reversed: that happens for small $\gamma$, when the kernel varies slowly.

options.text: Each training point influences only a tiny neighbourhood, so the boundary becomes very wiggly and the model tends to overfit
options.why: $K$ drops to almost 0 except for very close pairs, so the decision function is a sum of narrow bumps around the training points.

options.text: The penalty on slack variables increases
options.why: That is the role of $C$; $\gamma$ sets the kernel width.

options.text: $K(x, z) \to 1$ for every pair, so all points look identical
options.why: That is the limit $\gamma \to 0$. As $\gamma \to \infty$, $K \to 0$ for every pair with $x \ne z$.

questions.solution:
1. Large $\gamma$ makes $\exp(-\gamma\lVert x - z\rVert^2)$ fall off very quickly with distance.
2. Each support vector then shapes the boundary only near itself: low bias, high variance.

questions.stem: A function $K$ is evaluated on two points $x_1, x_2$, giving the matrix $G = [K(x_i, x_j)]$. Which of the following could be the Gram matrix of a valid (Mercer) kernel?

options.text: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$
options.why: Symmetric with eigenvalues 3 and 1, both positive.

options.text: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$
options.why: $\det = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0$, so one eigenvalue is negative ($-1$): not PSD. Also $|K(x_1,x_2)| \le \sqrt{K(x_1,x_1)K(x_2,x_2)}$ fails.

options.text: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 \\ 0.4 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$
options.why: Not symmetric: $K(x_1, x_2) = \phi(x_1)^\top\phi(x_2)$ must equal $K(x_2, x_1)$.

options.text: $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$
options.why: Symmetric with eigenvalues 5 and 0: PSD (singular is allowed), e.g. $\phi(x_1) = 2$, $\phi(x_2) = 1$.

questions.solution:
1. A valid kernel's Gram matrix must be symmetric and positive semidefinite.
2. For a symmetric 2×2 matrix: PSD $\iff$ diagonal entries $\ge 0$ and $\det \ge 0$.
3. Option 1: $\det = 3$, passes. Option 2: $\det = -3$, fails. Option 3: not symmetric. Option 4: $\det = 0$, passes.

questions.stem: A kernel SVM with RBF kernel $K(x, z) = \exp(-\lVert x - z\rVert^2)$ (so $\gamma = 1$) has two support vectors: $s_1 = (0, 0)$ with $y_1 = +1$, $\alpha_1 = 1$, and $s_2 = (1, 1)$ with $y_2 = -1$, $\alpha_2 = 1$; the bias is $b = 0$. The decision value $f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i K(s_i, x) + b$ at $x = (0, 0.5)$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Ignored the labels $y_i$ and added both kernel values.
Used the distance $\lVert x - z\rVert$ instead of its square in the exponent.
Swapped the labels of the two support vectors.
